subject: English
title: Sentence Structure
source: English Sentence Structure Study Guide + English Review slides (Do Now, practice, exit tickets)
notes: The PDF doesn't give the test date for the Sentence Structure test — set it under Grown-ups → Tests.

lesson.title: Subject & predicate
lesson.html:
Complete subject: who or what the sentence is about.
Complete predicate: what the subject does or is.
The little brown dog | barked at the mailman.

lesson.title: Fragments & run-ons
lesson.html: A fragment is missing a subject, predicate or complete thought. A run-on joins two complete sentences with no punctuation or conjunction. Fix with a period, or a comma + conjunction.

lesson.title: Four jobs
lesson.html: Declarative tells (.). Interrogative asks (?). Imperative commands or requests (. or !). Exclamatory shows strong feeling (!).

lesson.title: FANBOYS
lesson.html: for · and · nor · but · or · yet · so. Joining two complete sentences? Put a comma before the conjunction.

lesson.title: Prepositions & agreement
lesson.html: under the table = prepositional phrase. Singular subject → singular verb; plural → plural. Words inside a prepositional phrase don't change the subject: The basket of apples IS on the table.

list.q: In “The little brown dog barked at the mailman,” what is the complete subject?
list.why: The complete subject is who or what the sentence is about.
list.hint: Ask: who or what is it about?

list.q: In “The little brown dog barked at the mailman,” what is the complete predicate?
list.why: The predicate tells what the subject does.

list.q: In “The tiny puppy chased a ball,” the complete subject is…
list.why: The tiny puppy is who the sentence is about.

list.q: In “My cousin rides her bike,” what is the complete subject?
In “My cousin rides her bike,” what is the complete predicate?
list.why: What does she do? rides her bike.

list.q: In “The three children built a sandcastle,” who or what is the sentence about?
list.why: The complete subject: The three children.

list.q: A complete sentence must have…
list.a: a subject, a predicate and a complete thought
list.why: Who or what + what they do + a complete thought.

list.q: Which is a complete sentence?
list.a: The birds are singing in the trees.
list.why: It has a subject, a predicate and a complete thought.

list.q: Is “After the rain stopped.” a complete sentence or a fragment?
Which is a fragment?
list.why: Near the river has no subject or predicate.

list.q: Fix the fragment: “Playing with my friends.”
list.a: I enjoy playing with my friends.
list.why: Add a subject and a predicate.

list.q: Fix the fragment: “Beside the tall tree.”
list.a: The dog slept beside the tall tree.
list.why: Add a subject and predicate to complete the thought.

list.q: What is a run-on sentence?
list.a: Two complete sentences joined without proper punctuation or a conjunction
w: A sentence that is too short
list.why: We went to the park we played on the swings is a run-on.

list.q: Which fixes the run-on “We went to the park we played on the swings”?
list.a: We went to the park, and we played on the swings.
w: We went to the park we played, on the swings.
We went to the park and. We played on the swings
We went to the park, we played on the swings
list.why: A period or a comma + conjunction fixes it.

list.q: Fix this run-on: “I fed the fish it swam away.”
list.a: I fed the fish, and it swam away.
w: I fed the fish it swam away.
I fed the fish, it swam away
I fed the fish and, it swam away
list.why: Comma + and joins two complete thoughts.

list.q: Which fixes a run-on?
What type of sentence asks a question?
list.why: Interrogative sentences ask and end with ?

list.q: What type of sentence gives a command or request?
What type of sentence tells or states something?
list.why: Declarative sentences tell and end with a period.

list.q: What type of sentence shows strong feeling or excitement?
Which end mark goes after “Where are my crayons”?
Which end mark goes after “How many stars can you see”?
Which end mark goes after “We are going to the library”?
Which end mark goes after “That roller coaster was amazing”?
What type of sentence is “Please close the classroom door.”?
What type of sentence is “That cake is huge!”?
What type of sentence is “My family went to the zoo yesterday.”?
What type of sentence is “Where did you put my backpack?”?
What type of sentence is “What a wonderful surprise!”?
What type of sentence is “Will you read this story to me?”
What type of sentence is “Put your name at the top.”
What type of sentence is “The birds are building a nest.”
Can an imperative sentence end with an exclamation mark?
list.a: Yes — a strong command can end with !
list.why: Most imperatives end with a period, but a forceful command can end with !.

list.q: Which end marks can an imperative sentence have?
Which are the seven FANBOYS conjunctions?
list.a: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
w: for, and, not, but, on, yes, so
far, and, nor, bat, or, yet, so
for, at, nor, but, or, yet, sun
list.why: FANBOYS: For And Nor But Or Yet So.

list.q: FANBOYS: which conjunction explains why?
FANBOYS: which conjunction adds information?
FANBOYS: which conjunction shows a difference?
FANBOYS: which conjunction gives a choice?
FANBOYS: which conjunction shows a result?
FANBOYS: which conjunction shows a surprising difference?
I wanted to play outside, ___ it started raining.
list.hint: Think about how the two ideas are connected.

list.q: Do you want an apple ___ a banana?
I put on my coat ___ it was cold.
When FANBOYS joins two complete sentences, you put a comma…
list.why: I was hungry, so I ate a sandwich.

list.q: Which is a compound sentence?
list.a: I can snap, but I can't whistle.
w: I can snap but can't whistle.
I like to read and write.
list.why: Two complete sentences joined by , + conjunction.

list.q: Which is NOT a compound sentence?
list.a: I like to read and write.
w: I like to read, and I like to write.
I can snap, but I can't whistle.
I was hungry, so I ate a sandwich.
list.why: Read and write is one subject doing two things, not two complete sentences.

list.q: Combine: “I was hungry. I ate a sandwich.”
list.a: I was hungry, so I ate a sandwich.
w: I was hungry so, I ate a sandwich.
I was hungry I ate, so a sandwich.
I was hungry, ate a sandwich so.

list.q: What does a preposition show?
list.a: How a noun relates to another word (like where or when)
list.why: under the table: under shows where.

list.q: In “The ball rolled under the table,” what is the preposition?
In “The ball rolled under the table,” what is the prepositional phrase?
list.why: It starts with the preposition and includes its object.

list.q: In “The book is on the desk,” what is the prepositional phrase?
In “The cat hid under the bed,” what is the prepositional phrase?
In “The girl with the blue backpack walked to school,” which is a prepositional phrase?
Which word is a preposition?
list.why: Prepositions: in, on, under, over, above, below, beside, between, behind, near, with, at, to, from, of, by.

list.q: Which word is a preposition?
The basket of apples ___ on the table.
list.why: The subject is basket (singular). Words in the prepositional phrase don't change the subject.

list.q: The flock of birds ___ flying south.
The children ___ excited.
The dogs ___ through the park.
The team ___ ready.
The stack of papers ___ on my desk.
The birds ___ chirping.
He ___ to school.
They ___ to school.
Singular subjects use ______ verbs.
list.why: Singular with singular, plural with plural.
